entries.modern_form: PIE *h₂elgʷʰ- 'to be worth, cost, earn' (Pokorny algʷh- 'verdienen, Gegenwert', IEW I 32-33)
entries.note: Root, language label and gloss are all correct and are exactly what Nourai's cited page says: Pokorny I 32-33 heads the entry 'algᵂh- ‚verdienen, Gegenwert‘' with Skt. árhati / arghá-, Av. arəjaiti / arəjah-, NPers. arzīdan, Gk. ἀλφή / ἀλφεῖν, Lith. algà; the same entry stands in Walde-Pokorny I 91 and Watkins 1985 ('algwh-. To earn, be worth. [Pok. algvh- 32.]'; the root was dropped from the current online AHD appendix). LIV² 263-4 and Cheung 2007 s.v. *Harj reconstruct the same root. THE ONE REAL PROBLEM ON THIS CHART is the varj / varəcah- material hung under this root: Av. varəcah- 'vital power, splendour' (Skt. várcas-, MP warč, NP varj, varjāvand) belongs to a different etymon, as Nourai's own cited sources (Horn 241 and Mo'in's footnote in Borhan-e Qate' 2265, which cites Bartholomae col. 1367) both say.

nodes.words: arej, arejah : value ; arejat-aspa : (with) valuable horses ; varejah, varecah : value
nodes.derivation: Av. arəj- 'to be worth' (3sg. pres. arəjaiti, Vidēvdād/Hāđōxt) and the es-stem arəjah- n. 'worth, price' continue PIE *h₂elgʷʰ- with the regular Indo-Iranian outcome *Harjʰ- > Iranian *Harǧ- (Skt. cognates árhati, arghá-); Bartholomae AiW gives 'arəjah- n. ‘Wert, Preis’' and 'arəja- 1) Adj. ‘wertvoll’'. Arəjaṱ.aspa- is a bahuvrīhi 'whose horses are of worth' (arəjaṱ, 3sg. injunctive of the same verb, + aspa- 'horse'), the name of a Hyaona (Chionite) prince and enemy of Vištāspa in Yt. 5.109, 9.30 and 17.50 — Nourai's 'owner of valuable horses' is a fair rendering. BUT varəjah-/varəcah- does NOT belong here: Av. varəcah- (Skt. várcas-, PIIr *wárčas-) means 'vital power, energy; splendour', and Bartholomae's only Avestan compound of it, as-varəcah-, is glossed 'der grosse Kraft, Tatkraft besitzt' (Yt. 19.57-58, of Fraŋrasyan), not 'value'. Nourai has merged two etyma that merely look alike in New Persian (arj ~ varj).

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt leaf 40-41 (pp.32-33) has 'av. arəjaiti ... arəjah- (es-St.) n. ‚Wert, Preis“' — supports arəj/arəjah. Pokorny says nothing about Arəjaṱ.aspa- and nothing about varəcah-, which he treats nowhere under this root.

consulted.note: 'arəjah- n. ‘Wert, Preis’'; 'arəja- 1) Adj. ‘wertvoll’ ... 2) m. ‘Wert’'; 'arəjaṱ.aspa- m. EN. eines Hyaona-Fürsten' (Yt. 9.30, Yt. 5.109) — supports the first two words. But at leaf 172 Bartholomae has 'as-varəcah- Adj. ‘der grosse Kraft, Tatkraft besitzt’', i.e. varəcah- = 'power', not 'value' — contradicts the third.
'*AVESTAN: arj- ‘to be worth’ — Liste: 10. Pres. them.: IND. 3sg. YAv. arəjaiti (H 1.5 f., H 1.8, H 1.10), INJ. 3sg. arəjaṱ (Y 50.10, Y 64.6, Yt 5.109)'. No varəcah- anywhere in the entry.
Watkins lists only Sanskrit arhati under the root; no Avestan forms are cited, so nothing bears on varəcah-.

nodes.derivation: arj / arz: Av. arəjah- n. 'worth' > MP arž / arz [ʾLCʾ] 'value, merit' (Nyberg: 'arž ... Av. (192) arəjah-; Paz. arža; NP arj, arz'; MacKenzie: 'arz ... worth, value') > NP arz and, with the regular NP ž/j doublet of MP ž, arj; Hübschmann PS §2 lists 'arj, arz ‚Werth“' together as showing initial a- kept before a consonant cluster. Derivatives: MP arzōmand > NP arjmand/arjumand (MacKenzie p.12; Nyberg 'aržōmand ... NP arjmand'), MP arzān(īg) 'worthy, valuable' > NP arzān, which in NP shifted 'worth its price' > 'affordable' > 'cheap' (hence Nourai's 'valuable, also worthless'); NP arzīdan, arziš < MP arz-. NOTE the JSON transliteration 'rzân' is a scan slip: the script ارزان and the book both read arzān. Arjāsp ارجاسپ = Av. Arəjaṱ.aspa- (Hyaona king) via MP Arzāsp; in the Šāhnāma he is turned into a Turanian king killed by Esfandiyār at Rōyīn-diž, and Borhan-e Qateʽ (p.97-98) gives just that story. varj ورج: DISPUTED as drawn. Horn no.1077 (p.241) derives NP verč/varj from 'aw. *varəcah- ... phlv. varč bezw. varj, varčōmand bezw. varjōmand; ai. várcas- ‚Glanz“', and Mo'in's own footnote at BQT 2265 says the same, citing Bartholomae col. 1367; MacKenzie has ²warz 'miracle, miraculous power' and warzāwand 'having miraculous power' = NP ورجاوند varjāvand. So varj, varjmand, varjāvand belong with far(r)/xwarrah 'divine glory', not with arj 'value' — even though Mo'in's Farhang-e Fārsī glosses ورج simply as '[په.] ارزش، ارج', which is what Nourai followed. The Ferdowsī line quoted on the chart ('نه تنها شه و خسرو کشور است / که شاه است و با ورج پیغمبر است') is printed verbatim in Mo'in's BQT footnote among the passages showing varj = 'divine glory'.

nodes.derivation: OP arjana- is genuinely attested — but only in Darius's Susa foundation charter DSf (arjanam DSf 41f, arjanam-šaiy DSf 23), and Kent glosses it 'ornamentation', a sense fixed by the Akkadian version's simmanû 'decoration'. Formally it is a -na- derivative of the root arj- 'be worth' (Kent's own comparanda: 'Cf. Av. pres. arəja- ‘be worth’, Skt. árhati, and Ars. Phl. arzān, NPers. arzān, Av. arəjah- ‘worth, value’, Skt. argha-'), i.e. 'the precious/valuable (material)'. So the word, the language label and the root are right; Nourai's bare gloss 'valuable' is the etymological rather than the attested meaning.

ref_check.note: SOD_pages.txt \f-leaf 155, printed p.90, entry 2274: 'ʾyzn C / ezan ©<OP arjana ©pl. -ī ... valuable, worthy'. Gharib herself writes the Old Persian form arjana with exactly Nourai's gloss.

consulted.where: Kent, Old Persian, Lexicon p.170 s.v. arjana-
consulted.note: 'arjana- sb. ‘ornamentation’, as shown by AKK.: si-im-ma-nu-u ‘decoration’ ... against Hz.’s ‘limestone’ ... Cf. Av. pres. arəja- ‘be worth’, Skt. árhati, and Ars. Phl. arzān, NPers. arzān, Av. arəjah- ‘worth, value’, Skt. argha-. — arjanam nsn. DSf 41f; arjanam-šaiy DSf 23.' Same root, different attested gloss.
Bartholomae's Old Persian section has no arjana- headword in the searchable OCR; the word is treated in Kent and in the Susa-charter literature.
Cheung lists Avestan, MP, Sogdian, Choresmian, NW-Iranian and Sanskrit forms but no Old Persian nominal derivative.

nodes.derivation: Sogdian ʾyzn / ʾyjn (Christian and Manichaean scripts), read ēzan, 'worthy, valuable'; Gharib's dictionary has it twice, at no. 2274 (p.90) and no. 2401 (p.95). The form goes back to Iranian *arǧ-āna- / *arǧiyana-: Sogdian lost the r of the *ar- cluster and fronted the vowel, giving ʾy- for older *ʾarz- (contrast the still-transparent Sogdian doublet ʾyrznw and Parthian aržān, MP arzān, all 'worthy'). Nourai's arrow makes it descend from OP arjana-, which is Gharib's note on p.90 ('©<OP arjana'); but on p.95 the same author reconstructs '*arǧyan-; Av. arəja-, Parth. arzān, MP arzān', i.e. an inherited East-Iranian cognate rather than a borrowing from Old Persian — which is what Cheung and modern Sogdian scholarship assume. Hence plausible: right word, right root, but the OP→Sogdian edge is a sister relation, not descent.

nodes.derivation: Gk. ἀλφεῖν is the (thematic) aorist infinitive of the defective verb ἀλφάνω 'to bring in, fetch (a price), earn', Homeric and Herodotean (e.g. of slaves ‘fetching’ a price). It continues the PIE root aorist *h₂élgʷʰ-t (Gk. ἦλφον), to which the nasal present ἀλφάνω was built secondarily — hence Pokorny's remark that ἀλφεῖν corresponds to Skt. árhati but was pushed into aorist function by the fuller present. Beside it stands the noun ἀλφή 'gain, produce' (= Lith. algà, OPruss. gen. ālgas 'wage'). The node hangs directly off the root, correctly: Greek did not take it from Iranian.

entries.note: Both halves of Nourai's gloss are quotations from his two cited sources. Pokorny I 33-34 heads the entry 'alu- (-d-, -t-) ‚bitter, Bier, Alaun“' (so does Walde-Pokorny I 91); Watkins/AHD heads it 'alu-. In words related to sorcery, magic, possession, and intoxication', so the chart's 'bitter, also used in words related to intoxication, magic and sorcery' is a faithful merger. Caveat for the whole entry: the connection of Latin alūmen to this root is only 'perhaps' in the modern literature — Ernout-Meillet call alūmen a 'terme technique d'origine obscure', and Watkins's current appendix lists only ale under alu-, dropping alum entirely.

nodes.words: Alŭmen : alum, a bitter salt of aluminum
nodes.derivation: Lat. alūmen, gen. alūminis n. 'alum' (first attested in Claudius Quadrigarius, 1st c. BCE; Pliny NH describes its medicinal use on wounds) is analysed as an -men noun on the stem *alū- 'bitter', so literally 'the bitter (stuff)', with the parallel derivative alūta 'alum-tanned leather'. The only close comparandum is the Sicilian Greek gloss ἀλυδοιμον· πικρόν (Sophron, in Hesychius), plus the Germanic/Balto-Slavic 'ale/beer' words. De Vaan's Etymological Dictionary of Latin (p.36) analyses it as *h₂elut- + -men, i.e. from the same stem as ale. Nourai's chart is therefore in line with Pokorny and Klein, but Ernout-Meillet call the word 'd'origine obscure', so this is a probable rather than a proven derivation. (The chart's macron placement 'Alŭmen' should be alūmen with long ū.) The gloss 'a bitter salt of aluminum' is anachronistic wording for a Latin word but factually describes potash alum, KAl(SO₄)₂.

nodes.derivation: The French link is real but mislabelled. What French actually contributed is alumine (Guyton de Morveau / the Lavoisier nomenclature, late 1780s-90s), the chemists' name for the earth Al₂O₃, itself formed on Lat. alumen; English took it as alumina. The element name was then coined in English by Humphry Davy — alumium 1808, then aluminum by 1812 — and the -ium variant aluminium was proposed in January 1811 in W. H. Wollaston's account of Davy's experiments and endorsed by the Quarterly Review (1812) as having 'a more classical sound'; French, like most European languages, adopted aluminium from there. So Lat. alumen > Fr. alumine > (Eng./ModL) aluminium > Fr. aluminium is the real chain, and modern French aluminium is a legitimate immediate source for the Persian word below — but 'French aluminium' as a direct derivative of Latin alumen, with no English step, is not what the sources say.

ref_check.note: The AHD entry for aluminum gives only '[ALUMIN(A) + -(I)UM.]' (checked at ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=aluminum); it derives the element name from alumina, and the IE appendix root alu- lists no alum/aluminium derivatives at all. It does not say the word is French.

nodes.derivation: Persian آلومینیوم / آلومینیم ālūmīniy(u/o)m is a 20th-century scientific loan taken with French phonetics (ālūmīnyom, not English ə-lü-mi-nəm), which fits the general route by which chemical and technical vocabulary entered Persian — through French, the teaching language of the Dār al-Fonūn and of Iranian science until the mid-20th century. Wiktionary records exactly the two spellings the chart has: آلومینیوم with the alternative آلومینیم (āluminiyom). The route Latin alumen > French > Persian is therefore right; only the intermediate English/ModL coining step is missing (see node 2).

nodes.derivation: Four of the five words are correctly from Latin alūmen: alum (late 14c.) via Old French alum/alun; alumina, ModL. from alumen (on French alumine); aluminum (Davy, by 1812) and aluminium (proposed 1811) from alumina + -(i)um. But ALE cannot descend from Latin alūmen as the chart draws it: OE ealu/alu continues Proto-Germanic *aluþ- (ON öl, OS alo), a sister formation to alūmen from the same PIE stem *alu-t-/*alu-, and the Lithuanian alús and OCS olu ‘beer’ are Germanic loans, not cognates. Klein's own entry, which Nourai cites, says precisely that ale is 'cogn. with L. alumen' — cognate, not derived. So the node's parent is wrong for one of its five words.

entries.note: The Sanskrit word is real and means what the chart says (Monier-Williams 146.3; attested MBh., Suśruta, Chāndogya Up.). Āmlaka is the by-form Klein prints as 'OI. āmlak'; both go with āmla- 'sour, acid' (the fruit is the sour Indian gooseberry), and the Malay name malaka of the same tree — from which the city and Straits of Malacca are named — is the same word. Nourai's whole four-step chain Sanskrit > Persian > Arabic > Medieval Latin > English is precisely Klein's entry and, behind it, Devic's; Wiktionary and Asbaghi agree.

nodes.derivation: Skt. āmalaka-/āmalakī- reached Persian with the usual Middle Indic-to-Iranian syncope of the medial vowel and loss of the final -ka: āmalaka- > *āmlak > MP *āmlag > NP آمله āmla/āmola, with the regular MP -ag > NP -a(h) outcome. The word entered Persian as a materia-medica term (the fruit is one of the three myrobalans of the compound tri-phalā, Arabic إطریفل). Asbaghi reconstructs the Middle Persian stage explicitly. The chart's extra spelling آمُلَج is the back-borrowed Arabicised form (muʿarrab) of the same word, which is exactly how Borhan-e Qateʽ presents it.

nodes.derivation: Arabic أَمْلَج ʾamlaj, the emblic myrobalan, is a Persian loan of the Sasanian/early-Abbasid medical vocabulary: Pers. āmla(g) was taken over with the final velar rendered as ج j (the regular Arabic substitution for Persian -g, cf. پهلوی barg > Ar. barj-type renderings) and fitted to the ʾafʿal pattern. It is standard in the Arabic pharmacopoeia — Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (1025) discusses الأملج as the base of Chinese sukk. Variants أملیج / أملیک are recorded. This is a one-way Indian>Persian>Arabic transfer, not a Persian>Arabic>Persian round trip, although Persian then re-borrowed the Arabicised آملج alongside its own آمله (the chart's 'extra' spelling).

nodes.derivation: Medieval Latin emblica / emblicus is the Latin translators' form of Arabic amlaj, taken not from Classical Arabic but from an Egyptian-Arabic pronunciation āmleg (Klein), whence the -g- appears as -c- and a prothetic e- develops before the cluster; the word entered Latin through the 11th-13th-century translations of Arabic materia medica (al-Rāzī's Continens, Avicenna's Canon) made in Salerno, Toledo and southern Italy, alongside the other myrobalans chebulus, bellericus, indus. Old Occitan amblic/emblich and Old Spanish ambliçi are parallel Romance takes on the Arabic word.

nodes.derivation: English emblic (also emblic myrobalan) is taken straight from the Medieval Latin drug name emblica/emblicus of the apothecaries, and denotes Phyllanthus emblica (formerly Emblica officinalis), the Indian gooseberry, whose dried astringent fruit was used against dysentery; French emblique, Italian emblico and Spanish emblico are the same borrowing. The English word therefore carries a chain Sanskrit āmalaka- > Persian āmla > Arabic amlaj > ML emblica > English emblic, exactly as the chart draws it.
